newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Feb 26.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong Newspaper Headlines-Feb 26.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- MING PAO -- Research showed the Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa's popularity recovered after he announced that all the present Chinese government directors could keep their positions after the handover.

-- The number of Hong Kong people learning Mandarin Chinese language has grown dramatically this year. The number of people signed up to take the annual Mandarin open examination reached 911 this year, compared to 200 five years ago. But because most Hong Kong people were eager for quick results, the "instant Mandarin" they had learned was of a Cantonese style.

-- EXPRESS NEWS -- Pro-democracy activists said Jiang's speech showed a hint of a softening attitude towards the 1989 pro-democracy movement. Some believed the Chinese government would one day re-value the movement.
-- SING TAO DAILY -- Beijing sources said Chinese Communist Party elder Peng Zhen's health had deteriorated dramatically recently and he might die any time.

-- ECONOMIC JOURNAL -- The Sino-British Joint Liaison Group on the Hong Kong handover has agreed to invite international auditors to audit the accounts of Hong Kong's foreign currency reserves between April and June before the handover to China.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- Hongkong Telecom would put to an early test the new World Trade Organisation agreement on opening up international telecommunications markets, by applying to operate certain services in the United States.
-- Market sources said that red chip Guangdong Investment was hoping to list its brewery business on the Hong Kong stock exchange in July to celebrate the handover.
-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- New figures showed small brokers were a growing force in the Hong Kong stock market, riding high on their big-spending retail clients, while the big firms' stake had shrunk.
-- Tax partners of four major auditing firms said Hong Kong needs to provide more incentives to stay competitive in the region.
